title: SAMSON ASKED GOD FOR STRENGTH ONE LAST TIME—AND PULLED THE TEMPLE DOWN
paragraphs: SAMSON ASKED GOD FOR STRENGTH ONE LAST TIME—AND PULLED THE TEMPLE DOWN

They took his eyes. They took his freedom. They turned the man who once terrified armies into entertainment. But standing between two pillars, Samson discovered something terrifyingly beautiful: failure may destroy what you thought your life would become, but it does not place you beyond the reach of the God you desperately need.
There is a sentence in Samson's story that should frighten anyone who thinks yesterday's anointing guarantees today's obedience.
Samson woke up expecting everything to work like it always had.
It didn't.
He had escaped before.
He had broken ropes before.
He had walked away from impossible situations before.
He had experienced supernatural strength so many times that perhaps strength itself had begun to feel normal.
Then came one of the saddest statements in Scripture:
"...he did not know that the LORD had left him." — Judges 16:20
Read that slowly.
He got up expecting yesterday's strength...
and discovered that something had changed.
There are people reading this who understand that sentence more personally than they want to admit.
You still know the worship songs.
You still know when to say amen.
You still know how to post the verse.
You can still sound strong when somebody asks how you're doing.
But somewhere behind the Christian vocabulary, something has grown cold.
Prayer became occasional.
Compromise became explainable.
Conviction became inconvenient.
And the thing that once terrified you gradually became something you learned to tolerate.
That is part of what makes Samson's story so uncomfortable.
His collapse didn't begin between the pillars.
It began long before the temple fell.

Samson had been set apart before his birth. Judges 13 describes the extraordinary announcement surrounding him. He would be a Nazirite to God, and he would begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines.
God had given him calling.
God had given him strength.
God had given him opportunities few human beings would ever receive.
Yet extraordinary gifting did not make Samson immune to ordinary temptation.
That matters.
Because sometimes the most dangerous moment in your spiritual life isn't when you know you're weak.
It's when you've been strong for so long that you start believing you can play with weakness.
Samson kept walking toward what should have made him run.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Then Delilah entered the story.
People often reduce Samson and Delilah to a lesson about choosing the wrong relationship. There is truth there, but the wound goes deeper.
Delilah kept pressing.
Samson kept revealing.
The boundary kept moving.
Eventually the secret connected to his Nazirite consecration was exposed, his hair was cut, and the Philistines seized him.
They gouged out his eyes.
They bound him.
They took the warrior who had struck fear into his enemies and made him grind grain in prison.
Think about the humiliation.
The man who had followed what pleased his eyes could no longer see.
The man who could not easily be bound was now chained.
The man famous for supernatural strength was treated as powerless.
Sin has a brutal way of promising freedom while quietly manufacturing chains.
Maybe your chains don't look like Samson's.
Maybe nobody can see yours.
Maybe it's pornography that keeps calling you back after you promised God it was over.
Maybe it's bitterness.
An affair.
Secret messages.
Pride.
Alcohol.
Greed.
Envy.
A double life.
An obsession with being admired.
A relationship you know keeps pulling you farther from Christ.
Maybe you're not scandalously rebellious at all.
Maybe you're simply spiritually numb.
You don't hate Jesus.
You've just slowly learned how to live without needing Him very much.
And perhaps that is what scares you most.
But buried inside one of the darkest chapters of Samson's life is a tiny sentence.
It would be easy to read past it.
Don't.
"But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved." — Judges 16:22
His hair...
began...
to grow again.

That sentence is not permission to romanticize Samson's sin. His hair was not a magical battery, and Scripture had already explained that the LORD was the true source behind Samson's extraordinary strength.
But narratively, that quiet detail whispers into the darkness.
The story isn't finished.
Samson couldn't see it.
His enemies probably didn't fear it.
There was no thunder.
No army gathering outside.
No dramatic announcement.
Just hair growing quietly on the head of a broken man.
Sometimes restoration begins like that.
Quietly.
Before anybody applauds.
Before your circumstances change.
Before you feel powerful again.
Repentance often begins where performance finally dies.
The Philistine rulers eventually gathered for a great sacrifice to Dagon. They celebrated because they believed their god had delivered Samson into their hands.
Samson became entertainment.
The mighty man was brought out to be mocked.
Imagine standing there blind.
Hearing laughter you cannot locate.
Knowing people are staring at the wreckage of the person you used to be.
Knowing some of your suffering came through the choices you made.
There is a particular kind of pain in consequences you helped create yourself.
You can't blame everyone else.
You can't rewrite what happened.
You can't return to yesterday and become the person you should have been.
And that's where some people decide God could never want them again.
But Samson prayed.
Not an impressive prayer.
Not a long prayer.
Not a polished prayer.
A desperate one.
The Hebrew of Judges 16:28 preserves the cry:
זָכְרֵנִי נָא וְחַזְּקֵנִי נָא אַךְ הַפַּעַם הַזֶּה
Zokhreni na, vechazzekeni na, akh happa'am hazzeh.
"Please remember me, and please strengthen me, just this once."
Look at those words.
זָכְרֵנִי — zokhreni — "remember me."
וְחַזְּקֵנִי — vechazzekeni — "strengthen me."
Samson had finally reached a place where raw human strength could do nothing for him.
Blind.
Humiliated.
Surrounded.
At the end.
And now the strongest man in the story asks God for strength.
There is something profoundly revealing about that.
Samson's final strength would not come from Samson.
It would have to come from God.
He placed himself against the central pillars supporting the structure.
Then he pushed.
Judges says the building fell upon the Philistine rulers and the people gathered there, and that those who died with Samson were more than those he had killed during his life.

This is a severe scene of judgment within the unique history narrated in Judges. It is not a Christian instruction manual for revenge. Samson himself explicitly speaks of vengeance for his eyes, and Scripture is honest enough not to sanitize the complexity of its deeply flawed deliverer.
The Bible doesn't need perfect human heroes.
Because ultimately, the Bible is pointing us toward Someone better.
Samson can save Israel only partially.
Jesus saves completely.
Samson's life ends beneath the ruins.
Jesus enters death and rises victorious over it.
Samson's final victory involves the death of his enemies and himself.
Jesus does something infinitely more astonishing: He gives Himself for sinners who were His enemies so that His enemies can become His family.
That is where Samson's story must eventually drive the Christian heart.
Not toward admiration of physical destruction.
Toward hunger for the greater Deliverer.
Jesus Christ.
Samson was betrayed for silver.
Jesus was betrayed for silver.
Samson was mocked by his enemies.
Jesus was mocked.
Samson was handed over.
Jesus was handed over.
But Jesus was not a morally compromised savior finally trying to repair His mistakes.
He was the sinless Son of God willingly giving Himself for ours.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die because sin finally defeated Him.
He died to defeat sin.
And He rose.
That changes the question.
The question is no longer merely, "Can God give me another chance?"
The deeper question is:
"What has Christ already done for people who have ruined their chances?"
The Gospel answers:
Grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls darkness light.
Not grace that pats sin on the shoulder and tells you to continue.
Grace that forgives...
and then calls you out of the grave.
Maybe you have been thinking your scandal is the final chapter.
Your divorce.
Your addiction.
Your sexual failure.
Your betrayal.
Your secret.
Your years of lukewarm Christianity.
Your wasted calling.
Your hypocrisy.
Your collapse.
Your prison may be different from Samson's, but perhaps you've been grinding around the same emotional circle thinking:
God used me once.
God loved me once.
I was close once.
I prayed once.
I had fire once.
But look at me now.
Listen carefully.
You do not need Samson's physical strength.
You need Samson's realization:
You cannot save yourself.
And unlike Samson, you are not being called to pull down a building.
You are being called to come to Jesus.
To repent.
To stop defending what God is exposing.
To stop calling bondage freedom.
To stop hiding behind Christian language.
To bring the ugly truth into the light.
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — 1 John 1:9
Not some unrighteousness.
All.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Samson's eyes did not suddenly return.
His imprisonment wasn't erased as though nothing had happened.
Biblical grace is bigger than pretending consequences don't exist.
Grace means your consequences do not have the authority to become your savior, your identity, or your god.
Jesus does.
Maybe the prayer you need tonight isn't complicated.
"Jesus, remember me."
There is another place in Scripture where a dying man essentially prayed that prayer.
A criminal hanging beside Christ looked toward the crucified King and said:
"Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom." — Luke 23:42
And Jesus did not answer:
"You discovered Me too late."
He didn't demand a lifetime of religious accomplishments the dying man could no longer produce.
Jesus promised him paradise.
Do not misunderstand this.
That is not permission to postpone repentance.
It is proof of how astonishing Christ's mercy is when a sinner genuinely turns to Him.
You may have wasted years.
You may have damaged relationships.
You may carry scars for the rest of your earthly life.
But if you are still breathing, do not confuse "I cannot undo yesterday" with "Jesus cannot redeem what remains."
Those are not the same sentence.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted Christians.
The thief had nothing left to offer but faith.
And the Gospel keeps announcing the same scandalous reality:
Jesus saves sinners.
That means you should never turn Samson's last prayer into an excuse to keep compromising because "God will restore me later."
No.
The mercy of God should make you run from sin, not schedule more of it.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to perform for the people reading this.
But perhaps you do need to stop hiding from God.
You don't have to publish the details.
God already knows them.

Let the comments become more than engagement. Let believers pray for believers. Let people who thought they were the only ones struggling discover they are standing beside other sinners who desperately need the same Savior.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to give up tonight.
Not because Samson was perfect.
Because someday you may wake up feeling like your worst chapter has disqualified you from every chapter that could follow, and you may need to remember:
The God of Scripture is not intimidated by ruins.
Invite your family.
Send it to the person who thinks they have fallen too far.
Invite the lukewarm Christian back toward the fire.
Invite even the unbeliever who believes Christianity has nothing to say to broken people.
Because Christianity begins with the devastating admission that we are broken people who cannot rescue ourselves...
and the breathtaking announcement that a Savior came looking for us.
Samson stood blind between two pillars and discovered that his strength had never ultimately belonged to him.
Maybe that's what some of us need to discover before grace can rebuild what pride destroyed.
Your greatest tragedy may not be that you became weak.
It may be that you spent years believing you were strong without God.
And your greatest hope is not that you can become the old version of yourself again.
Your hope has a name.
Jesus Christ.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Confess what needs confession.
Seek reconciliation where reconciliation is possible.
Get accountable.
Walk away from what keeps dragging you toward darkness.
Come home.
And when shame whispers, "Look what you did," don't answer by pretending it didn't happen.
Look toward the cross and say:
"Look what Jesus did."
That is the difference between shame and the Gospel.
Shame says your worst moment gets the final word.
The Gospel says Jesus does.
So when you remember Samson, don't remember only the collapsing pillars.
Remember the prayer of a broken man who finally knew where strength came from.
זָכְרֵנִי נָא וְחַזְּקֵנִי נָא
"Remember me... strengthen me."
And then remember the greater Savior who doesn't merely give broken sinners enough strength for one final moment.
He gives them Himself.
Because maybe someone else needs to see that Christians aren't people with spotless histories.
We're people whose only hope is a spotless Savior.
And never forget this:
Your ruins may explain where you have been, but when you surrender them to Christ, they do not get to decide where grace will take you.
